narrative:
The model predicted a 75.2% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year in law school was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. This single piece of information had the largest impact on the model’s view of your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA came next. At 3.20 it sits only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, and this modest difference worked in your favor, gently pulling the prediction toward passing. However, its positive effect was not large enough to offset the other signals.

Your first-year class rank was the third most important factor. Like your third-year rank, you again placed in the second decile, well below the sixth-decile average of accepted applicants. This further increased the model’s estimate of bar exam failure.

Taken together, the two low class ranks outweighed the small benefit from your undergraduate grades, leading to the rejection.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your class standing in the remaining law school years, seek targeted bar-prep support, and consider reapplying once your later academic record shows clearer upward progress.
